claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vandenberg and Ryan, 2013.

claims.claim: EAAT3, EAAT4 and EAAT5 are expressed in neurons.
claims.source: EAAT3, EAAT4 and EAAT5 are expressed in neurons, whereas EAAT1 and EAAT2 are mainly present in astrocytes, where they are enriched in astrocyte terminal processes that form tripartite synapses with neurons and where they take up approximately 90% of released glutamate.
claims.evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about EAAT expression patterns.

claims.claim: EAAT1 and EAAT2 are mainly present in astrocytes and take up approximately 90% of released glutamate.
claims.source: EAAT3, EAAT4 and EAAT5 are expressed in neurons, whereas EAAT1 and EAAT2 are mainly present in astrocytes, where they are enriched in astrocyte terminal processes that form tripartite synapses with neurons and where they take up approximately 90% of released glutamate.
claims.evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about EAAT1 and EAAT2 function.

claims.claim: Glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity can trigger bulk Ca2+ influx into postsynaptic neurons via NMDA receptors.
claims.source: Glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity can trigger bulk Ca2+ influx into postsynaptic neurons via NMDA receptors, which causes mitochondrial Ca2+ overload, along with other cellular responses, and which subsequently generates excess amounts of ROS (Peng and Jou, 2010; Prentice et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Peng and Jou, 2010; Prentice et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Dysregulation of neural circuit activity can initiate subsequent disruption of the integrity of other constituents in the same network, resulting in overall circuit dysfunction and even neurodegeneration.
claims.source: Notably, it has emerged that dysregulation of neural circuit activity can initiate subsequent disruption of the integrity of other constituents in the same network, resulting in overall circuit dysfunction and even neurodegeneration (Fornito et al., 2015; Hussain et al., 2018; Palop and Mucke, 2010; Shababi et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Fornito et al., 2015; Hussain et al., 2018; Palop and Mucke, 2010; Shababi et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Coordinated animal behaviors are linked to the activity of spinal cord central pattern generators (CPG).
claims.source: Coordinated animal behaviors are linked to the activity of spinal cord central pattern generators (CPG), which are known to be specialized circuits that integrate inputs from the central brain and sensory neurons, and that subsequently generate rhythmic and patterned outputs to motor neurons (Kiehn, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kiehn, 2016.

claims.claim: The Drosophila feed-forward locomotor circuit has served as an appropriate model for exploring the pathogenic network mechanisms that underlie neurodegenerative diseases.
claims.source: The Drosophila feed-forward locomotor circuit has served as an appropriate model for exploring the pathogenic network mechanisms that underlie neurodegenerative diseases (Held et al., 2019; Imlach et al., 2012; Lotti et al., 2012), because it has a relatively simple neural circuitry compared to mammals yet retains conserved functions (Clark et al., 2018; Kohsaka et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Held et al., 2019; Imlach et al., 2012; Lotti et al., 2012; Clark et al., 2018; Kohsaka et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Drosophila Eaat1 is the sole Drosophila homolog of human EAAT2.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity due to depletion of Drosophila Eaat1, the sole Drosophila homolog of human EAAT2 (Besson et al., 2000), can induce a circuit-dependent ROS feedback loop that impairs the proper activities of the locomotor CPG circuit and muscles, ultimately leading to motor neuron overexcitation, abnormal NMJ growth and strength, and compromised movement.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Besson et al., 2000.

claims.claim: Depletion of Drosophila Eaat1 can induce a circuit-dependent ROS feedback loop that impairs the proper activities of the locomotor CPG circuit and muscles.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity due to depletion of Drosophila Eaat1, the sole Drosophila homolog of human EAAT2 (Besson et al., 2000), can induce a circuit-dependent ROS feedback loop that impairs the proper activities of the locomotor CPG circuit and muscles, ultimately leading to motor neuron overexcitation, abnormal NMJ growth and strength, and compromised movement.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experimental data.

claims.claim: Alterations in synaptic structure and function have been associated with a wide range of chronic neurodegenerative diseases.
claims.source: Alterations in synaptic structure and function have been associated with a wide range of chronic neurodegenerative diseases (Chand et al., 2018; Dachs et al., 2011; Fischer et al., 2004; Kariya et al., 2008; Lepeta et al., 2016; Rocha et al., 2013; Sharma et al., 2016; Wishart et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: The eaat1hypo mutant allele contained an insertion of a roo transposon in the last intron of the eaat1 locus, which results in a severe reduction of Eaat1 protein levels.
claims.source: The mutant allele contained an insertion of a roo transposon in the last intron of the eaat1 locus, which results in a severe reduction of Eaat1 protein levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D.

claims.claim: eaat1 null mutants (eaat1SM2/SM2) died before the first instar larval stage.
claims.source: Although eaat1 null mutants (eaat1SM2/SM2) died before the first instar larval stage, as reported previously (Stacey et al., 2010), approximately 20% of eaat1hypo/hypo animals developed almost normally during the larval stages, but most of them died at early pupal stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental observations and supported by a citation to Stacey et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Approximately 20% of eaat1hypo/hypo animals developed almost normally during the larval stages, but most of them died at early pupal stages.
claims.source: Although eaat1 null mutants (eaat1SM2/SM2) died before the first instar larval stage, as reported previously (Stacey et al., 2010), approximately 20% of eaat1hypo/hypo animals developed almost normally during the larval stages, but most of them died at early pupal stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: A majority of eaat1hypo/SM2 mutants died between the first and second instar larval stages.
claims.source: We noted that a majority of eaat1hypo/SM2 mutants died between the first and second instar larval stages, whereas ~1% of the mutants could further develop until the third instar stage, but they exhibited a significant ~10-day developmental delay (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: The expression levels of Eaat1 are correlated with successful larval development.
claims.source: These data indicate that the expression levels of Eaat1 are correlated with successful larval development.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing developmental outcomes with different Eaat1 levels.

claims.claim: eaat1hypo mutants displayed an ~50% increase in bouton number compared to wild-type controls.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 1A–D, eaat1hypo mutants displayed an ~50% increase in bouton number compared to wild-type controls, but their boutons were significantly smaller.
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1A–D.

claims.claim: eaat1hypo mutant boutons were significantly smaller than wild-type controls.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 1A–D, eaat1hypo mutants displayed an ~50% increase in bouton number compared to wild-type controls, but their boutons were significantly smaller.
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1A–D.

claims.claim: Overall presynaptic area, active zone number per NMJ, and muscle surface area in controls and eaat1hypo mutants were indistinguishable.
claims.source: Overall presynaptic area, active zone number per NMJ, and muscle surface area in controls and eaat1hypo mutants were indistinguishable (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claims.claim: eaat1hypo mutants showed an increase in the EJP amplitude and quantal content (QC).
claims.source: Compared to controls, eaat1hypo mutants showed an increase in the EJP amplitude and quantal content (QC) (Figure 1E–G), whereas the amplitude and frequency of miniature EJPs were comparable between controls and eaat1 mutants (Figure 1H; not shown for frequency), suggesting that loss of eaat1 also abnormally increases neurotransmitter release.
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1E–G.

claims.claim: The amplitude and frequency of miniature EJPs were comparable between controls and eaat1 mutants.
claims.source: Compared to controls, eaat1hypo mutants showed an increase in the EJP amplitude and quantal content (QC) (Figure 1E–G), whereas the amplitude and frequency of miniature EJPs were comparable between controls and eaat1 mutants (Figure 1H; not shown for frequency), suggesting that loss of eaat1 also abnormally increases neurotransmitter release.
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: Loss of eaat1 abnormally increases neurotransmitter release.
claims.source: Compared to controls, eaat1hypo mutants showed an increase in the EJP amplitude and quantal content (QC) (Figure 1E–G), whereas the amplitude and frequency of miniature EJPs were comparable between controls and eaat1 mutants (Figure 1H; not shown for frequency), suggesting that loss of eaat1 also abnormally increases neurotransmitter release.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological data showing increased EJP amplitude and quantal content.

claims.claim: Drosophila larval feed-forward locomotion is driven by the rhythmic activity of the locomotor CPG located in the ventral nerve cord (VNC).
claims.source: Drosophila larval feed-forward locomotion is driven by the rhythmic activity of the locomotor CPG located in the ventral nerve cord (VNC) (Cattaert and Birman, 2001), reminiscent of human and mouse spinal cords.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cattaert and Birman, 2001.

claims.claim: Motor neurons that are derived from dissected first instar larvae of the eaat1 null mutants receive sustained locomotor CPG output.
claims.source: It has been shown that motor neurons that are derived from dissected first instar larvae of the eaat1 null mutants receive sustained locomotor CPG output (Stacey et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stacey et al., 2010.

claims.claim: eaat1hypo motor neurons displayed a marked increase (~5 fold) in burst duration.
claims.source: By contrast, eaat1hypo motor neurons displayed a marked increase (~5 fold) in burst duration (Figure 1I–J).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1I–J.

claims.claim: Burst frequency and intra-burst spike density were decreased in eaat1hypo mutants relative to those in controls.
claims.source: Moreover, burst frequency and intra-burst spike density were decreased in eaat1hypo mutants relative to those in controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B.

claims.claim: Control and eaat1hypo motor neurons were fired for 0.28 ± 0.28 s and 22 ± 5.38 s, respectively, per recording minute.
claims.source: To represent the degree of sustained excitation on motor neurons quantitatively, we calculated the overall firing time of extremely long bursts (e.g. >15 s) for each recording minute and found that control and eaat1hypo motor neurons were fired for 0.28 ± 0.28 s and 22 ± 5.38 s, respectively (Figure 1K).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1K.

claims.claim: Wild-type control larvae displayed coordinated peristalsis and locomotion activity, whereas eaat1hypo mutants barely exhibited peristalsis and showed sluggish movement.
claims.source: Consistent with these results, wild-type control larvae displayed coordinated peristalsis and locomotion activity, whereas eaat1hypo mutants barely exhibited peristalsis and showed sluggish movement (Figure 1L–M).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1L–M.

claims.claim: Eaat1 is required to maintain proper patterning of the locomotor CPG output.
claims.source: Therefore, these data suggest that Eaat1 is required to maintain proper patterning of the locomotor CPG output, and its loss can alter the CPG output pattern, thereby eliciting excess stimulation of motor neurons.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing altered CPG output patterns in eaat1 mutants.

claims.claim: Drosophila Eaat1 is abundant in astrocyte-like glia of the central nervous system.
claims.source: Drosophila Eaat1 has been shown to be abundant in astrocyte-like glia of the central nervous system (Besson et al., 2000) (see also Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Besson et al., 2000 and data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Eaat1 is not present in the NMJ-associated glia throughout embryonic and larval development.
claims.source: Although glutamate is the major neurotransmitter utilized by Drosophila motor neurons, Eaat1 is not present in the NMJ-associated glia throughout embryonic and larval development (Rival et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rival et al., 2006.

claims.claim: The terminal processes of astrocyte-like glia were close to rather than part of the glutamatergic tripartite synapses.
claims.source: However, we noted that the terminal processes of astrocyte-like glia were close to rather than part of the glutamatergic tripartite synapses, which is consistent with a previous transmission electron microscopy study (Stork et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental observations and supported by a citation to Stork et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Eaat1 maintains glutamate homeostasis efficiently through its close synaptic association in the Drosophila central nervous system.
claims.source: Thus, Eaat1 maintains glutamate homeostasis efficiently through its close synaptic association in the Drosophila central nervous system.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing glutamate accumulation upon Eaat1 depletion.

claims.claim: Glial or astrocytic expression of the eaat1-venus transgene fully rescues the motor system defects in eaat1hypo mutants.
claims.source: This approach rescued the changes in locomotor CPG activity, NMJ boutons, and locomotion (Figure 2D–I and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B). In addition, a similar rescue effect was obtained with alrm-GAL4, an astrocyte-like glia-specific GAL4 driver (Doherty et al., 2009) (Figure 2D–I and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2D–I and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B.

claims.claim: Loss of Eaat1 in astrocyte-like glia leads to the defective motor system phenotypes.
claims.source: Thus, loss of Eaat1 in astrocyte-like glia leads to the defective motor system phenotypes.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments showing that glial or astrocytic expression of eaat1-venus rescues the motor system defects.

claims.claim: Neuronal expression of eaat1-venus in eaat1 mutants can restore premotor circuit activity and NMJ bouton growth but not locomotion.
claims.source: Interestingly, when we also tested the effect of neuronal expression of eaat1-venus, altered locomotor CPG output activity and NMJ boutons, but not impaired locomotion, were rescued (Figure 2D–I and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2D–I and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B.

claims.claim: Appropriate expression of Eaat1 in astrocytes is required to coordinate CPG activity between and/or within individual segments.
claims.source: This evidence suggests that the ectopic expression of Eaat1 in neurons can partially restore function, but appropriate expression of Eaat1 in astrocytes is required to coordinate CPG activity between and/or within individual segments.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments showing partial rescue with neuronal expression but full rescue with astrocytic expression.

claims.claim: Expression of the human EAAT2 (hEAAT2)-egfp transgene using repo-GAL4 rescued eaat1hypo mutant phenotypes.
claims.source: Next, we determined whether the functions of Drosophila Eaat1 are conserved in its human homolog. Expression of the human EAAT2 (hEAAT2)-egfp transgene using repo-GAL4 rescued eaat1hypo mutant phenotypes (Figure 2D–I), except for the reduced CPG burst frequency (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2D–I and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B.

claims.claim: The functions of EAAT are conserved from fly to human.
claims.source: Therefore, the functions of EAAT are conserved from fly to human.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments showing that human EAAT2 can rescue Drosophila eaat1 mutant phenotypes.

claims.claim: In Drosophila, the locomotor CPG network activates motor neurons via cholinergic and GABAergic interneurons.
claims.source: In Drosophila, the locomotor CPG network activates motor neurons via cholinergic and GABAergic interneurons (Figure 4D, top panel) (Rohrbough and Broadie, 2002), and motor neurons do not receive direct excitatory glutamatergic inputs (Kohsaka et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Rohrbough and Broadie, 2002 and Kohsaka et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Drosophila motor neurons do not receive direct excitatory glutamatergic inputs.
claims.source: In Drosophila, the locomotor CPG network activates motor neurons via cholinergic and GABAergic interneurons (Figure 4D, top panel) (Rohrbough and Broadie, 2002), and motor neurons do not receive direct excitatory glutamatergic inputs (Kohsaka et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kohsaka et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Drosophila can utilize glutamate as an inhibitory neurotransmitter that activates glutamate-gated chloride channel α (GluClα) to elicit Cl– influx.
claims.source: Moreover, Drosophila can utilize glutamate as an inhibitory neurotransmitter that activates glutamate-gated chloride channel α (GluClα) to elicit Cl– influx (Cully et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cully et al., 1996.

claims.claim: Glutamatergic period-positive median segmental interneurons (PMSIs) are responsible for relaying sensory inputs to motor neurons.
claims.source: Glutamatergic period-positive median segmental interneurons (PMSIs) are responsible for relaying sensory inputs to motor neurons (Clark et al., 2018; Kohsaka et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Clark et al., 2018 and Kohsaka et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Removal of one copy of gluClα did not modify the motor-system defects associated with eaat1hypo mutants.
claims.source: Nonetheless, removal of one copy of gluClα did not modify the motor-system defects associated with eaat1hypo mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), raising the interesting possibility that excess synaptic glutamate caused by loss of eaat1 may trigger excitotoxicity to alter locomotor CPG activity, which secondarily elicits excess stimulation of motor neurons.
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Expression of vglut-RNAi using OK371-GAL4 lowered excess perisynaptic glutamate in eaat1hypo mutants.
claims.source: Expression of vglut-RNAi using OK371-GAL4 lowered excess perisynaptic glutamate in eaat1hypo mutants (Figure 2B,C).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claims.claim: Expression of vglut-RNAi using OK371-GAL4 largely rescued the altered locomotor CPG activity and impaired locomotion of eaat1hypo mutants.
claims.source: Furthermore, it largely rescued the altered locomotor CPG activity and impaired locomotion of eaat1hypo mutants (Figure 3A–D; Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3A–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B.

claims.claim: The locomotor CPG circuit is assembled within the VNC.
claims.source: It has been shown previously that the locomotor CPG circuit is assembled within the VNC (Cattaert and Birman, 2001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cattaert and Birman, 2001.

claims.claim: Expression of UAS-eaat1-venus solely in the VNC of eaat1hypo mutants using teashirt(tsh)-GAL4 significantly reversed the prolonged CPG outputs.
claims.source: Consistently, when we expressed UAS-eaat1-venus solely in the VNC of eaat1hypo mutants using teashirt(tsh)-GAL4, it significantly reversed the prolonged CPG outputs (Figure 3A–C) and movement defects (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3A–C and Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Eaat1 expressed in the VNC may modulate the locomotor CPG output pattern, especially burst duration, to protect motor neurons from excess premotor excitation.
claims.source: Therefore, these results suggest that Eaat1 expressed in the VNC may modulate the locomotor CPG output pattern, especially burst duration, to protect motor neurons from excess premotor excitation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments showing that VNC-specific expression of eaat1-venus reverses prolonged CPG outputs.

claims.claim: Eaat1 expressed in the central brain may be responsible for triggering the motor CPG and perhaps tuning intra-burst spike density.
claims.source: Eaat1 expressed in the central brain may be responsible for triggering the motor CPG and perhaps tuning intra-burst spike density.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observation that VNC-specific expression does not rescue all CPG defects.

claims.claim: Glutamate excitotoxicity triggers bulk Ca2+ influxes to promote mitochondrial Ca2+ overload, overproducing ROS.
claims.source: It is known that glutamate excitotoxicity triggers bulk Ca2+ influxes to promote mitochondrial Ca2+ overload, overproducing ROS (Zeeshan et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zeeshan et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Increased ROS levels were evident in neuropils of eaat1hypo VNCs compared to controls.
claims.source: Compared to controls, increased ROS levels were evident in neuropils of eaat1hypo VNCs (Figure 4A–B).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4A–B.

claims.claim: After abrogating excitotoxicity by reducing gluRIID, the increased ROS were significantly neutralized.
claims.source: After abrogating excitotoxicity by reducing gluRIID, the increased ROS were significantly neutralized (Figure 4A–B), suggesting that glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity increases oxidative stress in the locomotor CPG circuit.
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4A–B.

claims.claim: Glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity increases oxidative stress in the locomotor CPG circuit.
claims.source: After abrogating excitotoxicity by reducing gluRIID, the increased ROS were significantly neutralized (Figure 4A–B), suggesting that glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity increases oxidative stress in the locomotor CPG circuit.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that reducing gluRIID neutralizes increased ROS.

claims.claim: Pan-neuronal expression of hSOD1 using nSyb-GAL4 eliminated the increased ROS in eaat1hypo mutants.
claims.source: Pan-neuronal expression of hSOD1 using nSyb-GAL4 eliminated the increased ROS in eaat1hypo mutants (Figure 4C) and also rescued the defects in locomotor CPG activity and larval movement (Figure 4D–G).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4D–G.

claims.claim: Excess ROS in neurons contributes to premotor circuit dysfunction in eaat1 mutants.
claims.source: These results provide evidence that excess ROS in neurons contributes to premotor circuit dysfunction in eaat1 mutants.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments showing that pan-neuronal expression of hSOD1 rescues CPG defects.

claims.claim: Expression of hSOD1 in glutamatergic neurons in eaat1hypo mutants using OK371-GAL4 did not reverse the increased ROS within the VNC or motor-system phenotypes.
claims.source: We first expressed hSOD1 in glutamatergic neurons in eaat1hypo mutants using OK371-GAL4. However, neither the increased ROS within the VNC nor those within the motor-system phenotypes were reversed (Figure 4C–G).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4C–G.

claims.claim: No rescue was observed when hSOD1 was expressed in GABAergic neurons using gad1-GAL4.
claims.source: Furthermore, no rescue was observed when hSOD1 was expressed in GABAergic neurons using gad1-GAL4 (Figure 4D–G).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4D–G.

claims.claim: Expression of hSOD1 in cholinergic neurons using cha-GAL4 led to a significant restoration of the ROS level, locomotor CPG activity, and locomotion.
claims.source: Remarkably, expression of hSOD1 in cholinergic neurons using cha-GAL4 led to a significant restoration of the ROS level, locomotor CPG activity, and locomotion, comparable to the effect of pan-neuronal hSOD1 expression (Figure 4C–G).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4C–G.

claims.claim: Targeted expression of hSOD1 in both bipolar and class I cholinergic sensory neurons using NP2225-GAL4 failed to affect the motor-system defects.
claims.source: However, targeted expression of hSOD1 in both these neuron subtypes using NP2225-GAL4 (Imlach et al., 2012) failed to affect the motor-system defects (Figure 4D–G).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4D–G.

claims.claim: Upon loss of eaat1, the excitotoxicity-induced ROS increase occurs in the cholinergic interneurons of the locomotor CPG network, dyregulating patterned locomotor CPG activity.
claims.source: Hence, upon loss of eaat1, the excitotoxicity-induced ROS increase occurs in the cholinergic interneurons of the locomotor CPG network, dyregulating patterned locomotor CPG activity.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments showing that hSOD1 expression in cholinergic neurons rescues CPG defects.

claims.claim: The Drosophila larval locomotor CPG circuit is assembled during the late embryonic stage.
claims.source: The Drosophila larval locomotor CPG circuit is assembled during the late embryonic stage (Kohsaka et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kohsaka et al., 2012.

claims.claim: eaat1 is functionally required during the larval stage but not during embryonic development when the CPG circuit is assembled.
claims.source: Thus, eaat1 is functionally required during the larval stage but not during embryonic development when the CPG circuit is assembled.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal rescue experiments showing that larval-stage expression of eaat1-venus rescues locomotion defects.

claims.claim: No overt changes in VNC architecture were observed in eaat1hypo mutants with regard to the number of neurons and astrocytes, the processes of astrocyte-like glia, and the dendritic field of motor neurons.
claims.source: Consistent with these results, we did not observe overt changes in VNC architecture in eaat1hypo mutants with regard to the number of neurons and astrocytes, the processes of astrocyte-like glia, and the dendritic field of motor neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Acute exposure of H2O2 phenocopies the prolonged burst duration of the motor CPG.

claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5C and F–G.

claims.claim: When the anti-oxidative ability of cholinergic neurons was enhanced by expressing hSOD1, the circuit effect of H2O2 was greatly diminished.

claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5C and F–G.

claims.claim: Upon loss of eaat1, a mild level of ROS does not perturb the synaptic connectivity of the locomotor circuit but instead alters its activity by influencing cholinergic transmission.
claims.source: Together, these data suggest that, upon loss of eaat1, a mild level of ROS does not perturb the synaptic connectivity of the locomotor circuit but instead alters its activity by influencing cholinergic transmission.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that ROS affects CPG activity without altering circuit architecture.

claims.claim: Oxidization of voltage-gated potassium channels caused by excess ROS can attenuate their inactivation, resulting in neuronal silencing under disease conditions.
claims.source: Oxidization of voltage-gated potassium channels caused by excess ROS can attenuate their inactivation, resulting in neuronal silencing under disease conditions (Sahoo et al., 2014; Sesti et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Sahoo et al., 2014 and Sesti et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Administration of 4-AP reversed prolonged CPG outputs induced by 0.006% H2O2 treatment.
claims.source: Nonetheless, 4-AP administration reversed prolonged CPG outputs induced by 0.006% H2O2 treatment (Figure 5C and F–G).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5C and F–G.

claims.claim: Acute 4-AP treatment alleviated the CPG output defect associated with the eaat1 mutation.
claims.source: In addition, acute 4-AP treatment alleviated the CPG output defect associated with the eaat1 mutation (Figure 5D and F–G).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5D and F–G.

claims.claim: Feeding eaat1hypo mutants with food containing 2 mM 4-AP throughout the larval stages abrogated the locomotion defect.
claims.source: Next, we fed eaat1hypo mutants with food containing 2 mM 4-AP throughout the larval stages. This manipulation also abrogated the locomotion defect (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: Treatment of eaat1hypo mutants with 15 μg/ml N-acetylcysteine amide (AD4) significantly corrected both premotor circuit dysfunction and compromised locomotion.
claims.source: Last, treatment of eaat1hypo mutants with 15 μg/ml N-acetylcysteine amide (AD4), a potent membrane penetrating antioxidant (Liu et al., 2015), also significantly corrected both premotor circuit dysfunction and compromised locomotion (Figure 5D–G).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5D–G.

claims.claim: The excitotoxicity-induced increase in ROS upon loss of eaat1 hampers the excitability of cholinergic interneurons, leading to premotor circuit dysfunction.
claims.source: Taken together, these findings strongly suggest that the excitotoxicity-induced increase in ROS upon loss of eaat1 hampers the excitability of cholinergic interneurons, leading to premotor circuit dysfunction.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that 4-AP and AD4 treatment rescue CPG defects.

claims.claim: The RFP/GFP ratio of mitotimer was significantly higher in eaat1hypo mutant muscles compared to control muscles, indicating an increased level of mitochondrial ROS.

claims.claim: The altered locomotor CPG activity due to loss of eaat1 can overexcite motor neurons and muscles, promoting oxidative stress in muscles.

claims.claim: Muscular expression of UAS-dsod1-RNAi using C57-GAL4 elevated ROS production in muscles but not in other tissues, such as the VNC.

claims.claim: The increased oxidative stress triggered by tonic motor neuron stimulation upon loss of eaat1 weakens muscle contraction and larval movement.

claims.claim: The ROS increase in the eaat1 mutant VNC was significantly relieved by means of 2 mM 4-AP treatment.

claims.claim: Excitotoxicity can induce oxidative stress in the locomotor CPG circuit and muscles and can lead to their dysfunction via a motor circuit-dependent mechanism.

claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that muscular expression of hSOD1 and 4-AP treatment affect CPG circuit ROS levels.

claims.claim: The feedback arising from inefficient muscle contraction sustains oxidative stress in the locomotor CPG circuit independently of glutamate release.

claims.claim: The excitotoxicity-induced ROS increase acts cell-autonomously to alter NMJ bouton formation upon loss of eaat1.

claims.claim: The conserved c-JUN-N-terminal kinase (JNK) stress signaling pathway is activated by increased oxidative stress to mediate a variety of cellular events, including differentiation, survival, and apoptosis.

claims.claim: The ROS-JNK axis positively regulates NMJ bouton growth in Drosophila.

claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Milton et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Motor-neuron-specific expression of the dominant-negative form of c-Fos (c-FosDN) rescued the bouton phenotype.

claims.claim: Reducing jra that encodes the Drosophila homolog of c-JUN had no effect on NMJ bouton phenotype.

claims.claim: Restoration of NMJ bouton morphology could further normalize the release probability of eaat1hypo mutant NMJs.

claims.claim: Premotor circuit dysfunction is the primary cause of NMJ bouton abnormalities and compromised locomotion upon loss of eaat1.

claims.claim: Glutamatergic transmission drives locomotor CPG activity and positively controls its output burst duration during larval movement.

claims.claim: Central brain removal of eaat1 reduced burst frequency, whereas VNC removal markedly extended burst duration.

claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing differential rescue effects of VNC-restricted eaat1-venus expression.

claims.claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of eaat1 extends PMSI-evoked inhibitory postsynaptic currents in motor neurons.

claims.claim: Upon loss of eaat1, glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity mainly contributes to locomotor CPG circuit dysfunction.

claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that reducing gluRIID rescues CPG defects.

claims.claim: A subset of cholinergic interneurons, which presumably constitutes the locomotor CPG circuit, is vulnerable to and influenced by the ROS increase.

claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that relieving ROS in cholinergic interneurons rescues CPG defects.

claims.claim: The effect of the ROS increase on circuit activity is acute and reversible.

claims.claim: ROS, especially those derived from mitochondrial respiration, act to strengthen the neuronal inhibition mediated by GABAA receptors.

results.result: The eaat1hypo mutant allele contains a roo transposon insertion in the last intron of the eaat1 locus, resulting in severely reduced Eaat1 protein levels. This reduction correlates with developmental viability: eaat1 null mutants (eaat1SM2/SM2) die before the first instar larval stage, ~20% of eaat1hypo/hypo animals survive to early pupal stages, and ~1% of eaat1hypo/SM2 mutants reach the third instar stage with significant developmental delay.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C29 are well-supported by molecular characterization (Western blot, immunostaining in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-D) and developmental viability data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E). The correlation between Eaat1 protein levels and developmental success is clearly demonstrated across multiple allelic combinations with appropriate controls.

results.result: Loss of eaat1 causes NMJ structural and functional alterations: eaat1hypo mutants display ~50% more boutons that are significantly smaller than wild-type controls, while overall presynaptic area, active zone number, and muscle surface area remain unchanged. Functionally, eaat1hypo mutants show increased EJP amplitude and quantal content, while miniature EJP amplitude and frequency are comparable to controls, indicating abnormally increased neurotransmitter release.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C35 are supported by comprehensive morphological (Figure 1A-D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-C) and electrophysiological data (Figure 1E-H). The combination of increased bouton number with smaller size, unchanged total presynaptic area, and increased evoked but not miniature EJPs provides converging evidence for altered NMJ structure and enhanced neurotransmitter release.

results.result: eaat1hypo mutants exhibit prolonged locomotor CPG output bursts (~5-fold increase in burst duration) with decreased burst frequency and intra-burst spike density. Control motor neurons fire for 0.28 ± 0.28 s per minute while eaat1hypo motor neurons fire for 22 ± 5.38 s per minute. This altered CPG output pattern correlates with severely impaired larval locomotion and peristalsis.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C42 are well-supported by electrophysiological recordings (Figure 1I-K, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-B) and behavioral assays (Figure 1L-M). The dramatic increase in burst duration and overall firing time, combined with decreased burst frequency and compromised locomotion, provides strong evidence that Eaat1 is required for proper CPG output patterning.

results.result: Drosophila Eaat1 is abundant in astrocyte-like glia of the CNS but not in NMJ-associated glia. Astrocyte-like glial processes are close to but not part of glutamatergic tripartite synapses. Glial or astrocytic expression of eaat1-venus fully rescues motor system defects in eaat1hypo mutants, while neuronal expression rescues CPG activity and NMJ bouton defects but not locomotion, indicating that appropriate astrocytic expression is required for coordinated CPG activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C50 are supported by immunostaining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), GRASP analysis (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), and comprehensive rescue experiments (Figure 2D-I, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-B). The differential rescue effects of glial versus neuronal expression provide strong evidence for the cell-type-specific requirement of Eaat1 function.

results.result: Expression of human EAAT2 (hEAAT2)-egfp using repo-GAL4 rescues eaat1hypo mutant phenotypes except for reduced CPG burst frequency, demonstrating functional conservation of EAAT from fly to human.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52 are supported by rescue experiments (Figure 2D-I, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-B) showing that human EAAT2 can largely substitute for Drosophila Eaat1. The partial rescue (all phenotypes except burst frequency) provides strong evidence for functional conservation while also revealing some species-specific differences.

results.result: Glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity, rather than inhibitory glutamatergic signaling, drives CPG dysfunction in eaat1 mutants. Reducing glutamate release (vglut-RNAi) or VNC-specific expression of eaat1-venus significantly reverses prolonged CPG outputs and movement defects. VNC-expressed Eaat1 modulates burst duration to protect motor neurons from excess premotor excitation, while central brain Eaat1 may control burst frequency and intra-burst spike density.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C63 are supported by genetic rescue experiments (Figure 3A-D, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The lack of rescue by reducing gluClα (C57) combined with rescue by reducing glutamate release (C58-C59) and region-specific rescue effects (C61-C63) provide strong evidence for excitotoxicity-mediated CPG dysfunction with anatomically distinct Eaat1 functions.

results.result: Loss of eaat1 increases ROS levels in VNC neuropils, which is neutralized by reducing gluRIID, indicating that glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity increases oxidative stress in the locomotor CPG circuit. Pan-neuronal expression of hSOD1 eliminates increased ROS and rescues CPG activity and locomotion defects, demonstrating that excess neuronal ROS contributes to premotor circuit dysfunction.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C69 are supported by ROS measurements (CM-H2DCFDA staining, Figure 4A-C) and genetic rescue experiments (Figure 4D-G). The reduction of ROS by blocking excitotoxicity (C66) and the rescue of motor defects by pan-neuronal antioxidant expression (C68) provide strong evidence linking glutamate excitotoxicity to ROS-mediated circuit dysfunction.

results.result: Expression of hSOD1 in cholinergic neurons (cha-GAL4), but not in glutamatergic (OK371-GAL4) or GABAergic (gad1-GAL4) neurons, significantly restores ROS levels, locomotor CPG activity, and locomotion in eaat1hypo mutants. Expression in cholinergic sensory neurons (NP2225-GAL4) fails to rescue, indicating that excitotoxicity-induced ROS increase occurs specifically in cholinergic interneurons of the locomotor CPG network.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C74 are supported by cell-type-specific rescue experiments (Figure 4C-G). The selective rescue by cholinergic but not other neuronal populations, combined with the lack of rescue by sensory neuron-specific expression, provides strong evidence for ROS accumulation in cholinergic CPG interneurons as the critical site of dysfunction.

results.result: Temporal rescue experiments demonstrate that eaat1 is functionally required during the larval stage but not during embryonic CPG circuit assembly. VNC architecture remains unchanged in eaat1hypo mutants. Acute H2O2 exposure phenocopies prolonged CPG burst duration in a dose-dependent manner, and this effect is diminished by expressing hSOD1 in cholinergic neurons, indicating that ROS alters circuit activity without perturbing synaptic connectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C80 are supported by GAL4/GAL80ts temporal rescue experiments (Figure 5A-B), VNC architecture analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and acute H2O2 exposure experiments (Figure 5C, F-G). The reversibility of the phenotype and the lack of structural changes provide strong evidence that ROS affects circuit function acutely rather than through developmental or structural alterations.

results.result: Administration of 4-AP (a K+ channel blocker) reverses prolonged CPG outputs induced by H2O2 treatment and alleviates CPG output defects in eaat1 mutants. Feeding eaat1hypo mutants with 2 mM 4-AP throughout larval stages abrogates locomotion defects. Treatment with the antioxidant AD4 also significantly corrects premotor circuit dysfunction and compromised locomotion, indicating that excitotoxicity-induced ROS hampers cholinergic interneuron excitability.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C86 are supported by pharmacological rescue experiments (Figure 5C-G). The rescue by both 4-AP (which enhances neuronal excitability) and AD4 (which reduces ROS) provides converging evidence that ROS-mediated reduction of cholinergic interneuron excitability underlies CPG dysfunction. The incomplete rescue with 4-AP feeding (~70% of animals) is appropriately noted.

results.result: eaat1hypo mutant muscles show increased mitochondrial ROS (elevated mitotimer RFP/GFP ratio) and elevated cytosolic ROS levels. This muscular ROS increase is normalized by reducing motor neuron inputs (reducing gluRIID) or by expressing hSOD1 in neurons (nSyb-GAL4 or cha-GAL4), indicating that altered locomotor CPG activity overexcites motor neurons and muscles, promoting oxidative stress in muscles.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C90 are supported by mitotimer measurements (Figure 6A-B) and CM-H2DCFDA staining (Figure 6C-E). The normalization of muscular ROS by interventions that correct CPG activity provides strong evidence that motor neuron overexcitation drives muscular oxidative stress. The specificity of rescue (nSyb-GAL4 and cha-GAL4 but not OK371-GAL4) strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Muscular expression of dsod1-RNAi elevates ROS production specifically in muscles, impairs muscle contractility, and compromises locomotion without affecting synaptic transmission or CPG activity. Muscular expression of hSOD1 in eaat1hypo mutants abrogates ROS increase and significantly improves locomotion, indicating that tonic motor neuron stimulation-induced oxidative stress weakens muscle contraction and larval movement.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C96 are supported by muscle-specific ROS measurements (Figure 5F), muscle contractility assays (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B), locomotion assays (Figure 6G-H), and electrophysiology (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-I). The selective effect on muscle function without affecting synaptic transmission or CPG activity provides strong evidence for ROS-mediated muscle weakness as a distinct component of the motor system defects.

results.result: Muscular expression of hSOD1 not only relieves ROS increase in muscles but also reverses ROS accumulation in the locomotor CPG circuit and prolonged circuit output. Treatment with 4-AP similarly reverses CPG activity and reduces VNC ROS without affecting perisynaptic glutamate levels. This indicates that inefficient muscle contraction attenuates sensory feedback inhibition, exacerbating premotor circuit dysfunction through a circuit-dependent ROS feedback loop independent of glutamate release.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C104 are supported by experiments showing that muscular hSOD1 expression (Figure 6I-L) and 4-AP treatment (Figure 4B, Figure 5D-E, Figure 6M) affect CPG circuit ROS and activity. The key observation that 4-AP reduces VNC ROS without affecting perisynaptic glutamate (C102) provides strong evidence for a glutamate-independent feedback mechanism. However, C98 is labeled as speculation, which is appropriate given the indirect nature of the evidence for sensory feedback involvement.

results.result: eaat1hypo mutant motor neurons exhibit increased mitochondrial ROS (elevated mitotimer RFP/GFP ratio), indicating that motor neuron overexcitation elevates oxidative stress. Correcting motor neuron excitation by 4-AP feeding or expressing hSOD1 in various neuronal populations (nSyb-GAL4, OK371-GAL4, D42-GAL4, cha-GAL4, C57-GAL4) or treating with AD4 rescues NMJ bouton phenotypes, demonstrating that excitotoxicity-induced ROS acts cell-autonomously to alter NMJ bouton formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C112 are supported by mitotimer measurements in motor neurons (Figure 7L-M) and comprehensive rescue experiments (Figure 7A-K). The rescue by motor neuron-specific hSOD1 expression (D42-GAL4) and the rescue by interventions that reduce motor neuron excitation provide strong evidence for cell-autonomous ROS effects on NMJ bouton formation.

results.result: Removal of one copy of bsk (JNK) or kay (c-FOS), or motor neuron-specific expression of c-FosDN, restores normal NMJ bouton morphology in eaat1hypo mutants, while reducing jra (c-JUN) has no effect. Restoration of NMJ bouton morphology normalizes release probability but does not affect CPG circuit dysregulation or compromised locomotion, indicating that ROS-activated JNK signaling cell-autonomously causes abnormal NMJ bouton formation, and premotor circuit dysfunction is the primary cause of motor system defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C120 are supported by genetic interaction experiments (Figure 7I-K) and functional assays (Figure 7N-P). The selective requirement for c-FOS but not c-JUN is consistent with prior work (C117). The key observation that restoring NMJ morphology does not rescue CPG dysfunction or locomotion (C118) provides strong evidence for the primacy of circuit dysfunction over NMJ structural changes.

results.result: Glutamate excitotoxicity due to Eaat1 depletion triggers a circuit-dependent ROS feedback loop that sculpts the motor system. Excitotoxicity initially elevates ROS, inactivating cholinergic interneurons and altering CPG output to overexcite motor neurons and muscles. Tonic motor neuron stimulation boosts muscular ROS, dampening muscle contractility, which feedback-enhances ROS accumulation in the CPG circuit and exacerbates circuit dysfunction. Excess premotor excitation promotes ROS-activated stress signaling that alters NMJ architecture. Under pathological conditions, impaired muscle activity serves as a key mediator for initiating the ROS feedback loop.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C5, C23, C136-C137 represent the central findings of the study and are supported by the comprehensive experimental evidence described in the previous results. The circuit-dependent ROS feedback loop is demonstrated through multiple lines of evidence: (1) ROS accumulation in cholinergic interneurons causes CPG dysfunction, (2) CPG dysfunction leads to motor neuron overexcitation and muscular ROS, (3) muscular ROS impairs muscle contractility, (4) impaired muscle contractility exacerbates CPG circuit ROS independently of glutamate, and (5) motor neuron ROS activates JNK signaling to alter NMJ structure. The integration of these findings into a coherent mechanistic model is well-supported.

results.result: Background knowledge claims establish the scientific context for the study, including: ROS generation and roles in physiology and pathology, glutamate neurotransmission and excitotoxicity, EAAT function and distribution, neural circuit dysregulation in disease, CPG function, Drosophila as a model system, NMJ structure-function relationships, and ROS-JNK signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C6-C24, C36-C37, C53-C56, C60, C64, C75, C81, C97, C105-C106, C113-C114 are background knowledge claims supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These claims provide essential context for interpreting the experimental findings. The citations appear appropriate and the claims are consistent with established knowledge in the field.

results.result: Discussion claims integrate current findings with prior work on glutamatergic regulation of Drosophila locomotor CPG circuits. VNC-restricted eaat1-venus expression reverses prolonged CPG output burst but not reduced frequency, indicating regional specificity of Eaat1 function. Reducing gluRIID but not gluClα rescues CPG defects, indicating excitotoxicity rather than inhibitory glutamatergic signaling drives dysfunction. Targeted relief of ROS in cholinergic interneurons alleviates CPG defects, and the effect is acute and reversible, suggesting temporal hypoexcitability of cholinergic interneurons underlies ROS-induced CPG dysfunction.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C131 are discussion/interpretation claims that integrate the experimental findings with prior literature. These claims are well-supported by the data presented in the study (particularly Figures 3-5) and appropriately cite relevant prior work. The interpretations are logical and consistent with the experimental evidence.

results.result: Discussion claims on ROS mechanisms in muscles and synapses: ROS strengthen GABAA receptor-mediated inhibition, modulate SERCA and RyR activity, oxidize myofilament proteins, and play roles in proprioceptive feedback and synaptic plasticity. Different ROS sources and temporal patterns may engage different signaling processes, as evidenced by differential requirements for c-FOS versus c-FOS/c-JUN in bouton outgrowth under different conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C142 are discussion claims that contextualize the findings within the broader literature on ROS signaling. These claims are appropriately supported by citations and provide reasonable interpretations of the differential signaling requirements observed in the study (e.g., c-FOS alone in eaat1 mutants versus c-FOS + c-JUN in dsod2 mutants). C141 is appropriately labeled as speculation.

results.result: Discussion claims on relevance to neurodegenerative diseases: EAAT2 downregulation occurs in Alzheimer's disease, ALS patients, and ALS rodent models. Spinal removal of mouse EAAT2 causes motor neuron death. Therapeutic interventions targeting EAAT2 or oxidative stress show variable efficacy. Drosophila Eaat1 depletion causes ALS-like characteristics. Neuronal hypoexcitability may be a shared mechanism in motor-related disorders, as evidenced by 4-AP efficacy in multiple conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C167 are discussion claims that relate the findings to human neurodegenerative diseases, particularly ALS. These claims are appropriately supported by citations to clinical and preclinical literature. The discussion appropriately notes the variable efficacy of therapeutic interventions (C150, C154) and the limitations of current approaches (C151-C153). C167 is appropriately labeled as speculation. The claims provide reasonable context for the potential translational relevance of the findings.

results.result: Eaat1 expressed in the central brain may be responsible for triggering the motor CPG and tuning intra-burst spike density.
results.evaluation: Claim C63 is speculative and based on the observation that VNC-specific expression of eaat1-venus does not rescue all CPG defects (reduced burst frequency and intra-burst spike density remain). While this suggests a role for central brain Eaat1, direct evidence for this function is not provided. The claim is appropriately labeled as speculation in the evidence type.
